title: Kimball Dimensional Modeling Techniques (consolidated 'official' techniques, drawn from The Data Warehouse Toolkit, 3rd Edition)
core_concepts: transaction / periodic snapshot / accumulating snapshot / factless fact tables
degenerate, role-playing, junk, snowflaked, outrigger dimensions
enterprise DW bus architecture and bus matrix
bridge tables for multivalued dimensions and ragged hierarchies
engineering_principles: Grain must be declared before dimensions/facts and is a binding contract; different grains must not be mixed in one fact table. Nulls are acceptable in measures but must be avoided in fact-table foreign keys (use a default dimension row). Every dimension gets an anonymous sequential integer surrogate key (date dimension exempt). Denormalize fixed-depth hierarchies into flat dimensions; avoid snowflakes; outriggers sparingly. Conformed dimensions are 'the essence of integration'; bus matrix rows are business processes, columns dimensions, implemented one row at a time. SCD2 rows need effective date, expiration date, current-row indicator.
practical_examples: Retail sales transaction grain (quantity and extended price allowed, store manager salary disallowed); order-fulfillment accumulating snapshot with a date FK per milestone; student-attends-class factless fact; patient multiple diagnoses via bridge table; date dimension keyed YYYYMMDD with a special unknown-date row; Type 7 dual views joined via durable vs surrogate key.
why_it_matters: This is the canonical statement of Kimball rules; a framework can cite it for MANDATORY grain/non-null-FK/surrogate-key rules and OPTIONAL pattern selection (junk, outrigger, bridge, fact surrogate keys).
authority_rationale: Published by the Kimball Group, the methodology's originating body, and explicitly labeled the 'official' techniques drawn from the 3rd edition of the defining book.
notes: PDF was fetched as binary and text-extracted locally with pdftotext. The HTML index of the same techniques (one page per technique) is https://www.kimballgroup.com/data-warehouse-business-intelligence-resources/kimball-techniques/dimensional-modeling-techniques/ (fetched; lists technique names only).

title: The 10 Essential Rules of Dimensional Modeling
core_concepts: date dimension on every fact table
engineering_principles: Rule 5: 'Fact table foreign keys should never be null'; many-to-many handled with a dual-keyed bridge table. Rule 8: 'Make certain that dimension tables use a surrogate key' (sequential, meaningless; date dimension exception) because surrogates shrink keys/indexes, are required for attribute history, and insulate against reused source keys. Rule 6: flatten fixed-depth hierarchies instead of snowflaking. Rule 9: conformed dimensions built once in ETL, blueprinted by the bus matrix. Rule 10: balance requirements and data realities.
practical_examples: Multiple diagnoses per encounter resolved with a bridge table; reused product numbers as the motivating case for surrogate keys; 'NA' default for null dimension attributes.
why_it_matters: The most compact normative list of Kimball rules, directly usable as MANDATORY/RECOMMENDED labels in a schema-design framework.
authority_rationale: Kimball Group official article by co-author of The Data Warehouse Toolkit.

title: The Data Warehouse Toolkit: The Definitive Guide to Dimensional Modeling, 3rd Edition (publisher page)
organization_author: Wiley; Ralph Kimball and Margy Ross
engineering_principles: Moves from fundamental design recommendations to complex scenarios; the 3rd edition adds updated star schema patterns, two new ETL chapters, and business matrices for 12 case studies.
practical_examples: Case studies in retail sales, inventory, procurement, invoicing, accounting, CRM, financial services, telecom, education, health care, insurance, e-commerce, big data analytics.
why_it_matters: Bibliographic anchor (ISBN 978-1-118-53080-1, 608 pages) for the Kimball rules cited in DWM-01/02.
authority_rationale: Publisher page for the recognized foundational book; the page itself carries only descriptive metadata.
notes: Table of contents not shown on page (linked as PDF only).

title: Differences of Opinion (Kimball bus architecture vs Corporate Information Factory)
organization_author: Kimball Group / Margy Ross (byline on page)
engineering_principles: Both approaches plan from an enterprise perspective and reject independent marts. CIF requires a 3NF layer before dimensional loading; Kimball considers duplicate storage of atomic data unwarranted in most cases and requires atomic data to be dimensionally structured because summary-only marts 'presuppose the questions'. Integration via conformed dimensions ('the backbone of any enterprise approach') rather than a normalized warehouse. Hybrid is viable but adds cost and delay.
practical_examples: Orders data copied into three departmental marts as the anti-pattern Kimball's process-centric modeling avoids.
why_it_matters: Primary-source statement of the Kimball side of the architecture debate; needed to document the conflict with Inmon fairly.
authority_rationale: Official Kimball Group article by a principal author of the methodology.
notes: A search snippet attributed the piece to Ralph Kimball (Intelligent Enterprise); the fetched page byline is Margy Ross. Follow-up de-escalation: Design Tip #139 'Much Ado About Nothing' (Margy Ross, DecisionWorks, 2011-10-05) https://decisionworks.com/2011/10/design-tip-139-much-ado-about-nothing/ (fetched) says 'Whatever approach you choose, embrace it' and that other approaches can succeed.

title: Building the Data Warehouse, 4th Edition (publisher page)
engineering_principles: Publisher description positions the 4th edition as the updated classic that 'launched the data warehousing industry', adding relational-vs-multidimensional design, unstructured data, and monitoring/testing.
practical_examples: None on the publisher page.
why_it_matters: Bibliographic anchor (ISBN 978-0-764-59944-6, 576 pages) for Inmon's foundational text; the four-property definition is sourced from Inmon's 2025 post (DWM-06) because the page does not reproduce it.
authority_rationale: Publisher page of the recognized foundational book; descriptive only.
notes: Page does not mention 'subject-oriented, integrated, time-variant, non-volatile' or CIF.

title: A Tale of Two Architectures - Kimball vs Inmon
subcategory: Inmon / Corporate Information Factory; Kimball vs Inmon debate
engineering_principles: Warehouse = 'subject oriented, integrated, non volatile, time variant collection of data for management's decision making'; it holds granular, historical, integrated data and is the only source for marts. Copying data into star-schema marts 'does not reconcile it'; conformed dimensions cover only some attributes, so MDM/golden records are needed. Simple dimensional model 'was never designed for enterprise integration'. Proposes a hybrid: central integrated warehouse feeding star-schema marts.
practical_examples: Large organizations ending up with many conflicting versions of the same value, redundant interface programs, shrinking refresh windows.
why_it_matters: Current (2025) first-person statement of Inmon's rules and his critique of Kimball; establishes the documented conflict and the accepted hybrid.
authority_rationale: Original author of the methodology writing on his own channel; self-published rather than refereed.
notes: Also quotes Kimball's definitions of a data warehouse ('a union of all the data marts'; 'a copy of the data specifically structured for query and analysis').

title: Bill Inmon's Data Lakehouse Collection (Building the Data Lakehouse 2nd Ed. and companions)
organization_author: Technics Publications; Bill Inmon with Ranjeet Srivastava and others
core_concepts: data lakehouse as next generation of warehouse and lake
engineering_principles: The lakehouse is 'the next generation of the data warehouse and data lake'; each of three data types needs its own foundation (data models, ontologies/taxonomies, distillation algorithms) for AI/ML and data mesh.
practical_examples: Deep dive into the Databricks Lakehouse Platform (2nd edition).
why_it_matters: Shows Inmon carrying the integrated-foundation premise of CIF into the lakehouse era rather than abandoning it.
authority_rationale: Publisher page for books by the methodology's originator; marketing copy without dates or ISBNs.
notes: First-edition data (Building the Data Lakehouse, Inmon/Levins/Srivastava, Technics Publications, October 2021, ISBN 978-1634629669) comes from WebSearch result listings (e.g., i-programmer.info), not from a fetched page.

title: Data Vault Business Value - Get Data from a Vault Easy DV2 (raw/business vault not for direct consumer access)
core_concepts: dimensional models, cubes, flat wide tables as marts
engineering_principles: 'The raw vault and business vault entities are not, or at least should not, be directly accessed by data consumers.' 'Report writers, analysts, and actuaries get what they need, consistently, from the Information Mart layer.' Direct vault access by data scientists is 'the exception, not the rule'. The Infomart layer may contain dimensional models, cubes, flat wide tables, web services and virtualization.
practical_examples: Critics complaining 'there are so many tables that people do not know where to start' answered by positioning the Infomart layer as the stable access point.
why_it_matters: Primary-source rule that Data Vault always implies a second, consumption-oriented model (usually Kimball), which decides how a framework routes BI workloads.
authority_rationale: Written by the inventor of Data Vault on the methodology's official body's site.
notes: Companion overview: 'Your Data Vault 2.0 Introduction - A Grounded Perspective' https://datavaultalliance.com/engineering/data-vault-2-0-an-introduction/ (fetched; published 2022-08-12, modified 2026-01-23; body credits Mark Budzinski, metadata lists Linstedt) states DV 2.0 aggregates best practices for 'methodology, architecture, and modeling', 'We load data in parallel', and keeps 'true, historical records of everything'.

title: How To: Test an Idea for Data Vault Standards
engineering_principles: Standards are not voted; proposals must be repeatable, pattern-based, non-conditional, scalable in batch and real time, measurable, auditable, cross-platform. Modeling standards must 'Not change the base definition of a Hub, a Link, or a Satellite', work in real time 'without structural changes, at up to 400k transactions per second', support big data (>300TB), 'hash keys, sequences, natural keys', CDC and backup/restore. Implementation must handle 1TB-500TB, be fault-tolerant and restartable, automatable for at least 98% of cases; platform-specific items are 'best practice', not standards; '30,000 test cases' back the basic standards.
practical_examples: 19 self-check questions (automation >=98%, restartable, auditable, scales without re-engineering, supports parallel teams and hybrid platforms).
why_it_matters: Defines what is MANDATORY (base object definitions, pattern repeatability, auditability) versus RECOMMENDED (hash keys, insert-only) in Data Vault 2.0, correcting vendor over-statements.
authority_rationale: Official standards-governance text by the methodology's inventor on the Alliance site.
notes: A guessed URL for a consolidated 'Data Vault 2.0 Standards' page returned 404. The Alliance's course page https://learn.datavaultalliance.com/cs/dv101-baseline-hands-on/ls/introduction-to-this-course/ (returned by WebSearch, not opened) states '100% insert driven best practice' and 'not using End-Dating is a best practice, NOT a standard'.

title: Building a Scalable Data Warehouse with Data Vault 2.0 (publisher page)
organization_author: Elsevier (Morgan Kaufmann imprint); Daniel Linstedt and Michael Olschimke
engineering_principles: Data Vault modeling is the technical warehouse layer built incrementally under the agile DV 2.0 methodology, with a stage layer below and dimensional information marts above; hashing is covered in extraction (Ch. 11), raw vault loading in Ch. 12, and loading the dimensional mart via the Business Vault, PIT and bridge tables in Ch. 14.
practical_examples: SQL Server Integration Services examples; Data Quality Services and Master Data Services in a Data Vault context; Meta Mart, Metrics Vault, Error Mart.
why_it_matters: Canonical book reference for DV 2.0 components; its chapter structure confirms marts are a distinct layer from the vault.
authority_rationale: Recognized book co-authored by the methodology inventor; publisher page is descriptive.
notes: Page lists both September 15 and September 29, 2015; ISBN 9780128025109 appears only in the ScienceDirect link.

title: Data Vault Glossary: Hub, Link, Satellite, Business Vault, and More
engineering_principles: Hash keys are primary keys of hubs and links and foreign keys from satellites; raw vault stores unmodified source data (auditable, no business rules); business vault applies business logic in the same structures; information marts are the delivery layer, usually dimensional and often virtualized as views; load date is arrival time (not event time) on every row; record source on every row; ghost records preserve referential integrity.
practical_examples: Customer number as business key; PIT pre-computing satellite timestamps per point in time; bridge pre-joining link paths.
why_it_matters: Compact, current component definitions from a co-author of the canonical DV 2.0 book, usable as the component vocabulary in a framework.
authority_rationale: Authored by Michael Olschimke, co-author of the canonical Data Vault 2.0 book; vendor/consultancy blog rather than the Alliance itself.
notes: Hash-key rationale: 'Hash Keys in Data Vault' (Marc Winkelmann, Scalefree, 2017-04-28, updated 2026-05-11) https://www.scalefree.com/blog/data-vault/hash-keys-in-the-data-vault/ (fetched) - hash derived 'without the need for a lookup in the parent table', enables parallel and cross-platform loads, hash diff for change detection, MD5 recommended, collision odds likened to 'a meteor landing on your data center', 'no silver bullet' (storage), rejects natural composite keys as PKs. Scalefree blog listing https://www.scalefree.com/data-vault/ (fetched) notes vanilla PostgreSQL struggling with DV joins at GB/TB scale.

title: Data Vault 2.0 - Introduction and (technical) differences with 1.0
engineering_principles: 'Hashes replace (integer) sequences/identity attributes everywhere as meaningless keys / surrogate keys'; 'you essentially don't have to do a key lookup for Hub and Link DWH/Surrogate keys anymore'; referential integrity 'cannot be enforced by ETL either, so it falls to housekeeping processing to manage RI (soft RI)'; hashes generated in the Staging Area so loads spread across MPP nodes.
practical_examples: Hub and Link loads running without key lookups; integration with NoSQL via hash of business key.
why_it_matters: Independent practitioner account of the DV 1.0 -> 2.0 key change and its RI trade-off, which a framework must weigh against Kimball's enforced-FK stance.
authority_rationale: Well-known Data Vault practitioner and automation author; personal blog.

title: Infographic: Data Warehouse and Data Vault Adoption Trends - Modeling, Modernization, and Automation
core_concepts: drawbacks: skills, implementation complexity, query performance, design complexity, multiple data versions
engineering_principles: Survey of 238 practitioners: drawbacks - skills and training 48%, implementation complexity 35%, query performance 32%, design complexity 29%, multiple versions of data 29%; technical drivers - extensibility 53%, scalability 40%, flexible architecture 35%; only 65% of adopters trained on DV 2.0; 31% fully / 60% partially aligned to standards; DV usage lags 3NF and star schema; 91% of best-in-class plan to increase DV role.
practical_examples: Comparative adoption of 3NF, star schema and Data Vault among respondents.
why_it_matters: The only quantified, analyst-run evidence found for Data Vault's documented criticisms (join/query performance, complexity, skills), needed for the tooling-maturity and query-complexity cells of the comparison matrix.
authority_rationale: Recognized analyst firms; survey-based, with undisclosed sponsor.
notes: Page gives no overall adoption percentage.

title: Oracle Database 21c Data Warehousing Guide - Chapter 2: Data Warehousing Logical Design (3NF vs star vs snowflake)
subcategory: 3NF enterprise data warehouse vs star schema
core_concepts: 3NF foundation layer plus star access layer
engineering_principles: 3NF 'seeks to minimize data redundancy and avoid anomalies', offers 'great flexibility' but 'very many tables... complex queries with many joins' ('over one thousand tables are commonly encountered'); star schema aims at 'structural simplicity and high performance data retrieval' and is what BI tools expect; snowflaking 'increases the number of dimension tables... reduced query performance'; 'Most data warehouses use a dimensional model'; 'the modern approach... does not pit star schemas and 3NF against each other' - 3NF as foundation EDW, star as access/performance layer; sensible denormalization in 3NF via views or slightly denormalized tables.
practical_examples: Facts such as sales measures with dimensions date, location, product; 3NF in Enterprise Data Warehousing environments, star in data marts.
why_it_matters: Vendor-neutral-sounding, official statement of when 3NF and star each fit; underwrites the two-layer (integration + presentation) pattern shared by Inmon, Oracle/Teradata and Data Vault.
authority_rationale: Official vendor documentation.
notes: Older edition with explicit rules also fetched: Oracle9i Data Warehousing Guide Rel. 2 (9.2), Ch. 17 'Schema Modeling Techniques', Part No. A96520-01, https://docs.oracle.com/cd/A97630_01/server.920/a96520/schemas.htm - 'Oracle Corporation recommends you choose a star schema over a snowflake schema unless you have a clear reason not to'; '3NF schemas are typically chosen for large data warehouses, especially environments with significant data-loading requirements that are used to feed data marts'; 3NF is 'neutral'; choice 'should be based upon the requirements and preferences of the data warehouse project team'. The 19c URL from the brief returned 404.

title: Teradata Retail Data Model (3NF enterprise model with Retail Analytic Schemas access layer)
core_concepts: third normal form industry data model
engineering_principles: 'The Retail Data Model (RDM) is a cross-functional third normal form data warehouse data model for retailers'; the Retail Analytic Schemas product 'includes dimensional data models and analytic data sets in one integrated data model' for the user access layer; rationale is 'a single, consistent view of data'.
practical_examples: Customers, stores, financials, products, inventory, employees subject areas in the 3NF model; RAS as predefined dimensional access layer.
why_it_matters: Evidence that a major MPP warehouse vendor ships a 3NF integration model paired with a dimensional access layer - the Inmon-style layering in commercial practice.
authority_rationale: Official vendor product documentation, though marketing-oriented and thin on rationale.
notes: Teradata technical documentation stating a normalized-model preference could not be retrieved from docs.teradata.com; only a training outline ('Normalized Data Model vs. Star Schema Model') surfaced in search.

title: Anchor Modeling - Agile Information Modeling in Evolving Data Environments (Data & Knowledge Engineering preprint)
organization_author: Lars Rönnbäck, Olle Regardt, Maria Bergholtz, Paul Johannesson, Petia Wohed (Resight, Teracom, Stockholm University DSV)
core_concepts: static vs historized vs knotted constructs
engineering_principles: 'changes in a data warehouse environment only require extensions, not modifications... all previous versions of the database schema are available as subsets of the current schema'; four constructs (anchor = set of entities; knot = fixed small set of values; attributes and ties in static/historized/knotted variants); 'a zero update strategy is used... only insert'; models are 'highly normalized... often even in 6NF' yet 'still offer fast retrieval' due to table elimination (requires declared PK/FK); lab tests show anchor databases 'under certain conditions... perform substantially better'; guidelines: historize only when versioning matters, split large ties so partial knowledge can be recorded.
practical_examples: Stage-performance example (actors, stages, programs, performances; gender knot; historized stage name; historized tie for stage location); production use since 2004 in insurance, logistics, retail, largest ~1 TB.
why_it_matters: Peer-reviewed definition of the most normalized warehouse method; shows the extreme end of the flexibility/auditability-vs-query-complexity trade-off and a direct counter-claim to 'denormalize for speed'.
authority_rationale: Peer-reviewed journal article by the method's creators (accepted in Data & Knowledge Engineering per Stockholm University notice; best paper award at ER 2009).
notes: PDF fetched as binary and text-extracted locally. Official site https://www.anchormodeling.com/ (fetched) is now a blog by Rönnbäck (2022 posts on transitional modeling/posits and SQL Server performance tests of 3.9-9.5 s on one million rows, with the author cautioning results may be skewed). Acceptance notice (search result, not opened): https://dash.dsv.su.se/2010/10/06/a-new-article-on-anchor-modeling/

title: What is the medallion lakehouse architecture?
engineering_principles: 'The medallion architecture describes a series of data layers that denote the quality of data stored in the lakehouse'; 'a data design pattern used to organize data logically'; layers 'incrementally and progressively improve the structure and quality of data'; following it 'is a recommended best practice but not a requirement'. Bronze = raw, original state; Silver = validated, cleaned, enriched (cleansing, deduplication, normalization; nested data via VARIANT or flattening into multiple tables); Gold = refined, aggregated, modeled 'using a dimensional model by establishing relationships and defining measures'.
practical_examples: weekly_bookings materialized view as a gold aggregate.
why_it_matters: Authoritative confirmation that medallion is a layering/quality convention orthogonal to Kimball/Inmon/Data Vault, so a framework should treat it as the hop structure within which the methodologies are applied.
authority_rationale: Official vendor documentation from the vendor that coined the term.
notes: Page makes no statement about Kimball/Inmon/Data Vault. Databricks blog 'Databricks Lakehouse Data Modeling: Myths, Truths, and Best Practices' (Shannon Barrow, Kyle Hale, 2025-12-15) https://www.databricks.com/blog/databricks-lakehouse-data-modeling-myths-truths-and-best-practices (fetched) adds: medallion is 'a reference architecture, not a mandatory structure'; 'Dimensional modeling principles thrive in the Lakehouse'; 'Leverage identity columns for surrogate key generation'; PK/FK constraints are informational, not enforced.

title: Data Warehousing Modeling Techniques and Their Implementation on the Databricks Lakehouse Platform
organization_author: Databricks / Soham Bhatt and Deepak Sekar
subcategory: Medallion mapping of Kimball, Inmon, Data Vault
core_concepts: Kimball star schema / Inmon marts in gold
engineering_principles: 'The Bronze layer uses the data models of source systems'; Data Vault 'typically fits well in the Silver layer' and silver 'has more 3rd-Normal Form like data models'; 'Kimball style star-schema based data models or Inmon style Data marts fit in this Gold Layer'; Kimball star schemas are 'pretty much the gold standard for the presentation layer'; 'Both normalized Data Vault (write-optimized) and denormalized dimensional models (read-optimized) data modeling styles have a place'; 'Sometimes tables in the Gold Layer can be completely denormalized' for feature engineering.
practical_examples: Layered lakehouse with Data Vault hubs/links/satellites in silver feeding star schemas in gold; fully denormalized gold tables for data scientists.
why_it_matters: The clearest vendor mapping of methodologies onto medallion layers; supports routing integration models to silver and consumption models (star/OBT) to gold.
authority_rationale: Major-vendor engineering blog by Databricks solution architects.
notes: Same-day companion: 'Prescriptive Guidance for Implementing a Data Vault Model on the Databricks Lakehouse Platform' (Bhatt, Shaikh, Wiebe, 2022-06-24) https://www.databricks.com/blog/2022/06/24/prescriptive-guidance-for-implementing-a-data-vault-model-on-the-databricks-lakehouse-platform.html (fetched): 'Data Vault modeling recommends using a hash of business keys as the primary keys'; 'Additional business ETL rules are not typically applied while loading the Raw Data Vault'; PIT tables 'bolster query performance as some satellites and hubs are pre-joined'; landing/staging = bronze; performance tips (Z-order on join keys, Bloom filters, 32-64 MB files, AQE because 'Data Vault models involve many joins').

title: Dimensional modeling in Lakeflow pipelines
subcategory: Kimball in the cloud lakehouse (keys, SCD2)
engineering_principles: 'Dimensional modeling is a technique for organizing your gold-layer data into fact tables and dimension tables'; prefer natural keys when stable; use a surrogate only 'when a source reuses or changes IDs'; 'Avoid hash-based surrogates like sha2(natural_key)' because hashing scatters adjacent rows and hurts liquid clustering / Z-order; derive order-preserving surrogates deterministically so they survive full refreshes; IDENTITY only for append-only, never-fully-refreshed tables; SCD2 via AUTO CDC 'STORED AS SCD TYPE 2'; facts as streaming tables fed from silver, dimensions as materialized views.
practical_examples: dim_date built with sequence() and explode(); dimensions as SCD Type 2 streaming tables when history is needed.
why_it_matters: Current vendor guidance that directly conflicts with both Kimball's mandatory integer surrogates and Data Vault's hash keys on a clustered lakehouse - a key conflict a framework must resolve by platform.
authority_rationale: Official vendor documentation.
notes: Covers only SCD Type 2; no SCD Type 1 discussion.

title: Is Kimball dimensional modeling still relevant in a modern data warehouse? (dbt Community Discourse thread)
core_concepts: outdated 'databases are slow and expensive' assumption
BI tools rely on fact/dimension concepts
Data Vault and Anchor Modeling alternatives
engineering_principles: Defenders: conformed dimensions prevent 'inconsistent results'; 'if facts share a grain, then widen your table' but mismatched grains cause 'gaps and duplicates'; logic should not live in the BI layer. Critics: 'Databases are slow and expensive' is outdated, warehouses are 'over engineered', formal modeling 'largely been a theatrical exercise'. Wide-table views: build one wide table per analysis requirement; counter: a single big table 'hits a wall at scale' and lacks a trainable pattern; hybrid proposal of normalized engineering layer plus flat tables for ~80% of use cases.
practical_examples: Customer list reused across every slice; wide table per analysis; Data Vault 2.0 with Kimball on top; practitioner reports of DV implementations being 'a mess'.
why_it_matters: Documents the actual arguments of the 'Kimball is dead?' debate at practitioner level and shows that the consensus retains grain and conformance while relaxing performance-motivated rules.
authority_rationale: Community forum posts by named but mostly unverified practitioners; useful for the shape of the debate, not as a normative source.
notes: Opening post is by 'claire' (2019-01-30), not Tristan Handy. The Coalesce 2020 talk by Dave Fowler (Chartio, 2020-12-12, 'Kimball in the context of the modern data warehouse: what's worth keeping, and what's not') and the Brooklyn Data counter-talk ('Babies and bathwater') could not be opened (404/redirect) and are known only from search summaries.

title: Building a Kimball dimensional model with dbt
organization_author: dbt Labs Developer Blog / Jonathan Neo (Canva), edited by Kenny Ning, reviewed by Paul Hallaste and Josh Devlin
subcategory: Kimball in the modern data stack
core_concepts: One Big Table for BI tools without relationships
engineering_principles: 'While the relevance of dimensional modeling has been debated by data practitioners, it is still one of the most widely adopted data modeling technique for analytics.' Fact tables 'represent a business process in the real world'; dimensions hold 'contextual or descriptive information'. Denormalize to a star to reduce consumer joins. Surrogate keys 'provide consumers... an easy-to-use key to join' and are generated by hashing (md5/hash) with dbt_utils. Build an OBT joining fact to all dimensions only when the BI tool lacks a semantic layer with relationships.
practical_examples: AdventureWorks sales process: fct_sales at order-detail grain with dim_product, dim_address, dim_customer, dim_credit_card, dim_order_status, dim_date; generate_surrogate_key(['productid']) in both dimension and fact; incremental materialization suggested for billion-row facts.
why_it_matters: Shows the dominant modern-data-stack tool's official stance: Kimball retained, surrogate keys implemented as hashes, OBT as a derived consumption artifact.
authority_rationale: Official dbt Labs developer blog (tool vendor), guest-authored and editorially reviewed.
notes: Does not cover SCD/dbt snapshots.

title: Star schema vs. OBT (benchmark on Redshift, Snowflake, BigQuery)
subcategory: One Big Table / wide denormalized tables
core_concepts: hybrid: star upstream, wide table downstream
engineering_principles: TPC-DS-derived test (store_sales plus 4 dimensions, BI-style aggregates, caching off): OBT faster than star by 25-30% on Redshift (10-45% on multi-node, 9 of 10 queries), ~25% on Snowflake (mixed; star won 3 queries), 49% average on BigQuery with star showing 'much higher variance'. Storage: Redshift disk 'from a bit over 30 gigabytes to over 90' (store_sales ~29.8 GB vs OBT ~60.3 GB). Recommendation: star for 'easier ELT code organization, easier navigation for analysts, or lower disk use'; OBT for small teams/single-subject speed; hybrid builds the star then re-joins into a wide table for end users.
practical_examples: Redshift dc2.large single-node ran out of disk when joining all dimensions into the OBT.
why_it_matters: Only measured OBT-vs-star evidence found; quantifies the speed gain and the storage cost that make OBT CONTEXTUAL rather than a default.
authority_rationale: Major data-tooling vendor engineering blog with disclosed methodology; not peer-reviewed.
notes: Author notes dbt could not set column compression on Redshift, so storage figures are likely worst-case.

title: The Rise of the Data Engineer ('Data modeling is changing' section)
organization_author: Maxime Beauchemin (creator of Apache Airflow and Apache Superset), published on freeCodeCamp
core_concepts: surrogate keys as a maintenance burden
dimension snapshots instead of complex SCD
engineering_principles: Star schema approaches 'are less relevant than they once were' because storage/compute are cheap and engineering time is scarce; 'further denormalization' and natural keys reduce joins; 'maintaining surrogate keys in dimensions can be tricky, and it makes fact tables less readable'; snapshotting full dimension copies each ETL cycle is 'a simple generic approach that requires little engineering effort' while complex SCD techniques 'are not intuitive and reduce accessibility'; conformance 'is still extremely important' but is now a tradeoff aligned gradually.
practical_examples: Full dimension snapshots per ETL cycle as the SCD alternative; data engineers as 'librarians' cataloging metadata.
why_it_matters: The most-cited practitioner origin of the 'Kimball is less relevant' position; identifies exactly which Kimball rules (surrogates, SCD machinery, star-for-performance) cloud teams relax.
authority_rationale: Well-known practitioner essay; influential but not an official body or refereed work.
notes: Companion essay 'Functional Data Engineering - a modern paradigm for batch data processing' (Medium, 2018-01-08; pure/idempotent tasks, immutable partitions, partition snapshots instead of SCD2) returned HTTP 403 at https://maximebeauchemin.medium.com/functional-data-engineering-a-modern-paradigm-for-batch-data-processing-2327ec32c42a and is NOT verified; its content is known only from search summaries. Data Council talk page returned by search but not opened: https://www.datacouncil.ai/functional-data-engineering-a-set-of-best-practices

title: Activity Schema Specification v2.0
core_concepts: required columns activity_id, ts, customer, activity, feature_json
temporal self-joins (First Ever, Last Before, First After, Aggregate In Between)
engineering_principles: 'An activity should never change'; 'A single entity cannot be identified with an email in one activity and a phone number in another'; 'All joins are self-joins to the activity_stream table, and they only use the entity and timestamp columns'; the model 'does not require any foreign key joins'; each activity keeps a consistent feature_json structure and stores only data it is authoritative for; entity tables are 'similar to dimension tables in a star schema'; 'Unlike dimensional modeling, activities should only store metadata that they are authoritative for.'
practical_examples: <entity>_stream naming; cohort activity defining result rows with appended relationships that never add or drop rows.
why_it_matters: A documented alternative to star schemas for single-entity behavioral analytics; its explicit rules let a framework scope it to event-sequence workloads and exclude multi-entity financial data.
authority_rationale: Published open specification with a named author, but originated and promoted by one vendor (Narrator) with limited independent adoption evidence.
notes: Project site https://www.activityschema.com/ (fetched) describes 'modeling all data in the warehouse as a single time series table' with 'no joins between models' and credits Ahmed Elsamadisi.

title: The Analytics Setup Guidebook - Data Modeling Layer & Concepts (and book index)
organization_author: Holistics / Huy Nguyen, Ha Pham, Cedric Chin
subcategory: Kimball in the modern ELT stack
core_concepts: Kimball / Inmon / Data Vault as classical approaches
engineering_principles: Data modeling is a layer mapping raw data to business terms with transformations run 'within the data warehouse, as per the ELT paradigm'; models are SQL SELECT statements over tables or other models; persisting models (equivalent to materialized views) is justified 'for performance reasons'; readers experienced in 'Kimball, Inmon or Data Vault-style data modeling' can skim because the approach is 'contemporary'.
practical_examples: Turning homestay.listings into a star schema via a modeling-layer tool.
why_it_matters: Represents the vendor-authored 'modern data stack' view that modeling moves into the warehouse as a SQL layer, within which Kimball structures remain a target rather than a mandate.
authority_rationale: Free vendor guidebook by Holistics staff; widely read but commercial and not refereed.
notes: Book index http://www.holistics.io/books/setup-analytics/ (fetched) lists chapter 3 sections 'Kimball's Dimensional Data Modeling' and 'How has data modeling evolved in modern cloud era?' but those section URLs could not be resolved (404), so Holistics' specific verdict on surrogate keys/SCD is not verified here.
